In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of ethanol on the fatty acid composition of the phospholipide fraction of human blood serum.
the study of fatty acids, their metabolism, and their role in the pathogenesis and treatment of liver diseases.
the effect of alcohol on the fatty acid profile of the serum and the separated lipid classes in alcohol users and patients with liver damage.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the plasma phospholipids from current ethanol abusers have a fatty acid pattern which is different from that of lifelong abstainers and patients with liver cirrhosis.
ethanol abuse and liver disease are associated with an increased level of linoleic fatty acid and a decreased level of palmitic acid in the phospholipoprotein fraction.
alcoholics have increased levels of linoleic and arachidonic acids in their blood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ethanol consumption is associated with increased levels of arachidonyl and linoleoyl phospholipids, and that this increase is associated with an increased level of diene-conjugates in the serum.
alcohol consumption is related to a significant increase of linoleic (LA) and arachidonic (AA) acids, and a decrease of palmitic (16:0) acid in the serum and phospholipids.

the plasma fatty acid profile of ethanol abusers and of patients with ethanol-related disease is characterized by an increased level of arachidonate and of diene-conjugates, and an increased proportion of linolenate in phospholipid and triglyceride fractions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are a lot of different types of fatty acids in the blood, and the ratio of these fatty acids changes in people with alcoholic liver disease.
the plasma fatty acid pattern is significantly changed in ethanol users and in patients with alcohol-related liver disease.
the use of alcohol can cause changes in your liver, including fatty liver disease.
